extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and reporters (learners of news-writing techniques)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporting and writing newspaper weather stories, including what topics to cover, how to place forecasts, tone choices (informative vs. lighter/humorous), and use of authoritative observational detail. Focused on practical news-writing for daily newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence of official forecasts
rubrics_metrics.description: "Official forecasts of the weather are given a place of prominence on the front page of most papers, and are read with interest by most readers.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place official forecasts prominently (often front page). Treat the forecast as a high-value item because it is widely read; use it as an anchor for weather coverage and link other stories to official predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize weather's effects on audiences' lives
rubrics_metrics.description: "The universal interest in the weather, which makes it the most common topic of conversation, is due to its effect upon health, business, and pleasure.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame weather stories around concrete impacts — health, commerce, agriculture, transportation, recreation — and tailor details to relevant reader groups (businessman, farmer, shopper, pleasure-seeker). Explicitly connect forecasts or events to these stakeholder concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects appropriate for weather stories
rubrics_metrics.description: "Besides the official reports, there is opportunity for weather stories of various kinds. The change of the seasons, extremes of heat and cold, storms, and unusual weather of any sort serve as subjects for weather stories.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select topics such as seasonal transitions, temperature extremes, storms, unusual phenomena (e.g., heavy snow in April). Use these recurring and exceptional phenomena as the basis for both routine and feature pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify eclipses as astronomical, not meteorological
rubrics_metrics.description: "Two stories of an eclipse of the sun have been included in this division, although, of course, such phenomena should be classed as astronomical rather than meteorological.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering events like eclipses, recognize and state their primary scientific domain (astronomy). Use appropriate scientific/astronomical sources and avoid treating these phenomena purely as routine weather events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of tone: informative versus lighter/humorous treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: "Although the purely informative type of story is the usual one for weather, the subject may be treated in a lighter vein. There is often a chance for life and color whether the treatment be informative or more or less humorous.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide tone based on audience and context: straight informative pieces for forecasts and hazards; lighter, colorful or humorous framing for human-interest or seasonal-feel pieces. Either approach should incorporate vivid detail and 'life and color' to engage readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use life, color, and human-interest details
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is often a chance for life and color whether the treatment be informative or more or less humorous.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enrich weather copy with anecdotes, scene-setting, sensory detail, and human reactions (crowds, commuters, businesses affected) as illustrated in the sample stories (e.g., crowds in parks, people with smoked glasses during an eclipse, traffic disruptions). Such details increase reader engagement and local relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use authoritative observational data and expert detail when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples in the eclipse stories give precise timings, names of observers, instruments, and photographic technique (e.g., first contact at 9:35:28, use of 40-foot photoheliograph, names of professors and assistants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For technically significant weather/astronomical events, include precise measurements, timings, and identify authoritative observers/institutions to lend accuracy and credibility. When technical procedures are relevant (photography of eclipse, instrument descriptions), explain them concisely for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt style to audience by showing different treatments of the same facts
rubrics_metrics.description: "Note — In the next two stories the facts about the same eclipse are given in different ways.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that the same factual event can be reported in multiple styles — straightforward, factual accounts versus witty or colorful narrations. Match the style to the paper's voice and the expected reader response; comparative examples are useful teaching tools.
